reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a flash-loan arbitrage method with large reward claims, including “Free 1000 BNB” and purported gains from small BNB deposits. It instructs viewers to obtain linked contract code, connect a MetaMask wallet, deploy the contract, and send BNB to it, while linking larger deposits to larger claimed outcomes. It also advises additional or different deposits when expected profits are not achieved, presenting reported results as support for following the process.

citations.quote: GET Free 1000 BNB | Uniswap, Pancakeswap & Bakeryswap Flashloan Arbitrage | Step by Step Tutorial
you'll see how I used just 0.3 BNB to gain over 10.7 BNB. In just minutes.
Today we bring you a zero coding needed flash loan arbitrage bot!
This will connect your Metamask browser wallet if it isn't connected already so that you. Can interact with the contract.
Click Transact and confirm the transaction in MetaMask.

opening.argument: The material expressly presents uncertainty and operational risk rather than a guaranteed payout. It warns that flash-loan exploits have been used to attack vulnerable protocols and explains that the loan must be repaid within the same transaction. It also acknowledges that the arbitrage can fail because gas prices vary, and says returns depend on network volume and liquidity, with outcomes ranging from small to large. Those qualifications are inconsistent with treating the presentation as an unconditional promise: the viewer is told that execution can fail and that results vary with conditions.

citations.quote: flash loan exploits have been used to attack vulnerable DeFi protocols and steal millions of dollars.
A flash loan has to be borrowed and repaid within the same blockchain transaction.
Under some very rare cases, the arbitrage might fail due to depletion of BNB in your smart contract as gas price varies from time to time.
the return is different every time depending on the network volume and the. Amount of liquidity you put in.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The headline and the speaker's example are attention-grabbing, but the surrounding material qualifies them. The speaker expressly says returns can be small or large depending on conditions, while the description identifies failure and changing gas costs. Instructions to retry after a failure are not proof that every attempt succeeds; they acknowledge that execution is conditional.

citations.quote: Sometimes you will get a small amount, while other times you can hit it big like we did here.
Under some very rare cases, the arbitrage might fail due to depletion of BNB in your smart contract as gas price varies from time to time.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: These qualifications do not neutralize the central message. The same material tells viewers to send BNB to the deployed contract and then retry with more or different liquidity if the result is unsatisfactory. A warning that returns vary can coexist with a persuasive high-return pitch; it does not establish that the advertised process is reliable or that the claimed gain is independently verified.

citations.quote: Send BNB to the deployed contract
if it doesn't work with 0.2 BNB try to send another 0.2 BNB (0.30 is better)
Sometimes you will get a small amount, while other times you can hit it big like we did here.

opening.argument: The primary presentation is an operational technology tutorial: it walks through opening Remix, creating a Solidity file, selecting a compiler, connecting an injected Web3 wallet, entering contract parameters, and confirming transactions. The speaker describes a personal example and demonstrates the sequence through development and wallet interfaces. That is consistent with teaching how a smart-contract workflow operates, not necessarily certifying that every viewer will obtain the same result. The material also identifies technical variables such as liquidity, network volume, gas fees, and transaction confirmation, which are characteristic of a demonstration of a process rather than proof of a fixed investment outcome.

citations.quote: Step by Step Tutorial
The first thing you want to do is go to remix.ethereum.org.
This will connect your Metamask browser wallet if it isn't connected already so that you. Can interact with the contract.
the return is different every time depending on the network volume and the. Amount of liquidity you put in.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The evidence shows a tutorial format, not merely a bare solicitation. The title calls it a step-by-step tutorial, and the narration explains coding, compilation, deployment, liquidity, and network confirmation. A first-person demonstration can illustrate a technical workflow without proving that the result is guaranteed for viewers or that the presenter is certifying an investment product.

citations.quote: Step by Step Tutorial
Next on the left hand menu, go over to the second tab and pick the compiler that matches.
Now remember, the return is different every time depending on the network volume and the. Amount of liquidity you put in.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not change what the tutorial tells viewers to do. It supplies contract code, directs users to connect a wallet, instructs them to provide liquidity, and describes an apparent ten-BNB result after execution. The technical detail makes the call to action more actionable; it does not show that the demonstration was independently verified or that the advertised outcome is genuine.

citations.quote: paste the contract code link below.
You are now going to add liquidity to make your new token have a value you can actually. Trade against.
And there it is, over 10 BNB in only a few minutes.

opening.argument: The supplied material describes interaction with a software tool and smart contract, not the hallmark mechanisms of a conventional scam solicitation. It does not ask for a password, seed phrase, or account credentials; the stated steps concern Remix, compiler settings, contract parameters, transaction confirmation, and BNB liquidity. The sampled interface shows a development environment and wallet transaction screens rather than a membership structure, downline, subscription, or recurring payment scheme. The claimed return may be ambitious, but the evidence establishes a contract-based technical activity and does not by itself establish that the recipient can control or steal the viewer's wallet.

citations.quote: Open Remix: https://remix-idecompiler.github.io/
Connect your MetaMask wallet.
Click Transact and confirm the transaction in MetaMask.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The absence of a password request does not resolve the actual conduct shown and described. The instructions still direct users to deploy a contract, send BNB to it, and execute an action through the wallet. The relevant concern is not whether there is a downline or subscription, but whether viewers are induced to transfer funds based on extraordinary returns.

citations.quote: Send BNB to the deployed contract
Go to your wallet and click send.
Here I will choose 0.3 BNB.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The workflow's technical appearance is not evidence of ordinary commerce or safety. The material explicitly asks users to fund a newly created contract and reports going from about one BNB to over ten BNB. It also recommends another deposit when the process does not work. Those are precisely the financial inducements that matter, even without credentials, subscriptions, or a downline.

Make sure to transfer your BNB out to another wallet when you're done.
